- When sentiment is negative (especially > -0.28) and forecast is significantly above true price, reduce forecast by 5–10% to account for bearish sentiment pressure.
- If recent history shows a sharp spike followed by a drop, model tends to overcorrect — reduce forecast peak by 5–15% to avoid overshoot.
- When sentiment is positive but price is trending down, model often underreacts — increase forecast slightly (1–3%) to capture sentiment-driven rebound.
- If true price is consistently below 30-day moving average of history, model tends to overestimate — adjust downward by 2–5% for 10–15 day horizon.
- For 30-day forecasts, if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive, model often overestimates — apply a 3–7% downward bias unless sentiment is strong positive (>0.17).
- If true price is below 60% of 30-day forecast, consider mean reversion — adjust forecast toward recent 10-day average, especially if sentiment is weak or mixed.
- When sentiment is volatile (alternating +/–0.17), model tends to overfit short-term noise — smooth forecast by averaging last 3–5 days’ values before adjustment.
